about: The driver's behaviour, as data rather than as prose.
A specification nobody can run is a specification every implementation reads
differently. So this file is what 'the Python binding is correct' means, and
the Rust driver runs exactly the same file - which is what stops the reference
implementation and the specification drifting apart, because there is only one
of them.
A runner is about forty lines in any language: open a scratch database, run
each case's setup, run each step, compare. drivers/README.md walks through it.
VALUES are one-key objects so that NULL and the empty string can never be
confused, which is the same reason the driver has a Null variant:
{"null": true}   {"int": 7}   {"real": 0.5}
A blob is a byte array rather than base64 so that no runner needs a decoder.
A STEP asserts whatever keys it carries and ignores the rest, so a case can
check a row count without pinning the rows, or a status without pinning the
message. The keys are:
sql               the statement (required)
params            values bound to ?1, ?2, ...
limit             rows to hand back; absent means all
columns           the result column names, in order
rows              every row handed back, in order
affected          rows changed; use null to assert it is a query
total             rows produced before the limit - exact, not an estimate
more              whether the limit cut anything off
status            the failure's status name; absent means it must succeed
message_contains  a substring of the failure's message
feature_contains  a substring of the construct named by an unsupported refusal

cases.name: insert_then_select
cases.about: The shape everything else rests on: a write reports what it changed, and a read gives it back.
setup: CREATE TABLE t (a INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, b TEXT)

steps.sql: SELECT a, b FROM t ORDER BY a

cases.name: every_value_kind_round_trips
cases.about: All five kinds, including the two that are easy to get wrong: a blob holding a NUL byte, and text that is not ASCII. A driver that renders values as text loses the first; one that uses C strings truncates it.
setup: CREATE TABLE v (k TEXT PRIMARY KEY, value BLOB)

steps.sql: SELECT value FROM v WHERE k = 'null'
SELECT value FROM v WHERE k = 'int'
SELECT value FROM v WHERE k = 'real'
SELECT value FROM v WHERE k = 'text'
SELECT value FROM v WHERE k = 'blob'

cases.name: null_is_not_the_empty_string
cases.about: The fault a grid drawing both as nothing would hide: a column never filled in and one filled in with nothing are not the same fact about a row.
setup: CREATE TABLE n (a INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, b TEXT)

steps.sql: SELECT b FROM n WHERE a = 1
SELECT b FROM n WHERE a = 2

cases.name: a_limit_cuts_the_rows_handed_back_and_total_stays_exact
cases.about: The engine materialises, so `total` was counted rather than estimated. That is what lets a grid say `1-2 of 5` and mean it.
setup: CREATE TABLE many (a INTEGER PRIMARY KEY)
INSERT INTO many VALUES (1)
INSERT INTO many VALUES (2)
INSERT INTO many VALUES (3)
INSERT INTO many VALUES (4)
INSERT INTO many VALUES (5)

steps.sql: SELECT a FROM many ORDER BY a
SELECT a FROM many ORDER BY a

cases.name: parameters_are_bound_not_pasted
cases.about: A value that would be syntax if it were pasted into the statement.
setup: CREATE TABLE p (a INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, b TEXT)

steps.sql: SELECT b FROM p WHERE a = ?1

cases.name: a_missing_table_is_not_found_and_a_typo_is_syntax
cases.about: The three refusals a caller has to be able to tell apart. This case and the next are the whole point of the driver.
setup: CREATE TABLE people (a INTEGER PRIMARY KEY)

cases.name: an_unimplemented_construct_refuses_by_name
cases.about: A construct the engine has not built reports `unsupported` and names itself, which is a different thing from a statement that is wrong. A binding that folds this into its general error type has thrown the design away. VACUUM is the example because it is still unimplemented; when it is built, repoint this at whatever still is rather than deleting the case.

cases.name: a_constraint_refuses_a_write
cases.about: A refusal that is the schema doing its job, and must not read as either a syntax error or a missing feature.
setup: CREATE TABLE u (a INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, b TEXT UNIQUE)
INSERT INTO u VALUES (1, 'one')

cases.name: a_transaction_commits_all_of_it
setup: CREATE TABLE c (a INTEGER PRIMARY KEY)

cases.name: a_rollback_undoes_all_of_it
cases.about: Including the row written before the one that failed, which is the half a driver that stopped at the first error but did not roll back would leave behind.
setup: CREATE TABLE r (a INTEGER PRIMARY KEY)
INSERT INTO r VALUES (1)

cases.name: a_savepoint_rolls_back_to_itself
setup: CREATE TABLE s (a INTEGER PRIMARY KEY)

cases.name: a_delete_that_matched_nothing_says_zero_rather_than_failing
cases.about: Zero changed rows is an answer, not an error. A row editor's rule that every statement must change exactly one row is built on being told the difference.
setup: CREATE TABLE d (a INTEGER PRIMARY KEY)
INSERT INTO d VALUES (1)

cases.name: returning_gives_rows_and_a_count
cases.about: The one statement that fills both, which is why `affected` is decided by the count rather than by whether there were columns.
setup: CREATE TABLE ret (a INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, b TEXT)

steps.sql: INSERT INTO ret VALUES (1, 'one') RETURNING a, b

cases.name: the_schema_can_be_read_back
cases.about: `sqlite_schema` is a readable table and it holds the CREATE statement as it was typed, which is what lets a consumer show a person what they wrote rather than something composed from a catalogue.
setup: CREATE TABLE shown (a INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, b TEXT)

steps.sql: SELECT type, name FROM sqlite_schema WHERE name = 'shown'
SELECT sql FROM sqlite_schema WHERE name = 'shown'

rows.text: CREATE TABLE shown (a INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, b TEXT)

cases.name: a_columns_declared_type_is_reported_and_an_expression_has_none
cases.about: An expression genuinely has no declared type, and the empty string is the honest answer rather than a guess taken from the first row - which would be a different answer on a different page of the same query.
setup: CREATE TABLE typed (a INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, b TEXT)
INSERT INTO typed VALUES (1, 'one')
